Problem 268. Crossing the fictional border network of Quartz
Knowledge context.
Political maps can be treated as adjacency networks. This lets us reason about border crossings without relying on memorized real-world geography.
Given facts.
Countries are represented by the fictional states Quartz, Grove, Fern, Zephyr, Elm, Juniper. Shared borders: Quartz–Grove, Grove–Fern, Fern–Zephyr, Quartz–Elm, Elm–Juniper, Juniper–Zephyr.
Rules.
Crossing one border corresponds to traversing one graph edge. A route may use only listed borders. A state is unavoidable only if every feasible route passes through it.
Task.
What is the fewest number of border crossings needed to travel from Quartz to Zephyr? Is Grove necessarily crossed?
Step-by-step solution.

1. Turn each shared border into an undirected link. 2. A shortest-link search gives distance 3 from Quartz to Zephyr. 3. Remove Grove and check whether Zephyr is still reachable from Quartz. 4. It is still reachable, so Grove is not unavoidable.
Answer.
3 border crossing(s); Grove is not unavoidable.
Knowledge takeaway.
Neighbourhood on a map is a graph relation; shortest routes and unavoidable transit points are different questions.
Formal model.
Undirected graph; shortest path length plus reachability after deleting a candidate vertex.

G5. Maps, legends, and clues
Problem 271. Reading a layered map legend (A1)
Knowledge context.
A map legend translates symbols into properties. One location may have several properties at the same time.
Given facts.

Legend: tree=forest, wavy line=river, double line=road, arch=bridge, square=village, triangle=hill. Cells: A1 has forest, road; A2 has bridge, river; B1 has forest, river, road; B2 has road, village.
